blocks.text: 1. Logging

blocks.alt: A request produces a log entry that gets stored

blocks.text: Monitoring covered tracking a production RAG system's health over time. Logging, recording what actually happened for each individual request, complements that aggregate view with the fine-grained detail of one specific request.
It writes a structured record of the query, retrieved chunks, and generated answer for every single request.
2. Monitoring Versus Logging

blocks.alt: Monitoring aggregates metrics while logging records individual events

blocks.text: Monitoring tracks aggregate system health over time, like average latency or error rate.
Logging instead captures the full detail of one specific request, available to inspect later.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Practice","What it captures"],"rows":[["Monitoring","Aggregate trends across many requests over time"],["Logging","Full detail of one specific individual request"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Structured Logs Are Actually Queryable

blocks.alt: An unstructured text log is compared against a structured JSON log

blocks.text: As with a strict JSON schema per function in Function Calling, a log written as structured fields can be filtered and searched later.
A free-form text log is far harder to query at scale than one with a consistent schema.
4. What To Log At Each RAG Stage

blocks.alt: A query goes through retrieval, then generation, each logged

blocks.text: The query, the retrieved chunk IDs, and the generated answer are each worth their own logged field.
Each stage of the pipeline leaves its own trace in the log record.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Pipeline stage","What gets logged"],"rows":[["Retrieval","Query text and retrieved chunk IDs"],["Generation","The final generated answer text"]]}

blocks.text: 5. Logging Enables Reconstructing A Failed Request
A detailed log record lets a developer reconstruct exactly what happened on a specific failed request.
Without that log, a one-off failure is nearly impossible to debug after the fact.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A user reporting one bad answer from yesterday can only be properly debugged if the query, retrieved chunks, and generated answer for that exact request were actually logged at the time.

blocks.text: 6. Logging Sensitive Data Requires Care

blocks.alt: Sensitive data gets redacted before logging

blocks.text: As with an answer that references a specific user's account details in Response Cache, raw queries and answers can contain personal or sensitive information.
Logging needs its own redaction or access control, not blanket unrestricted storage.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A query containing a customer's full account number, should be redacted before being written to a log file that many engineers can access, rather than stored in plain, unrestricted text.

blocks.text: 7. Log Volume Grows With Every Request
Every single request adds another log record, unlike a cache which reuses stored entries.
Log storage needs its own retention and rotation policy over time.
8. Correlation IDs Link Logs Across Stages

blocks.alt: A request ID links stage A log and stage B log

blocks.text: One request can touch several separate pipeline stages, each writing its own log entry.
A shared correlation ID ties all of those separate entries back to the same single request.
9. Recognizing When Detailed Per-Request Logging Is Worth Its Storage Cost

blocks.alt: Debugging complex failures points toward detailed logging

blocks.text: Debugging a specific reported failure needs detailed per-request logs.
Tracking overall system trends relies on monitoring's aggregate metrics instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates writing a structured log entry per stage with a shared correlation ID and basic redaction.

code.content:
import uuid

logs = []

def redact(text):
    # logging sensitive data requires care
    if "account number" in text.lower():
        return "[REDACTED: contains account number]"
    return text

def log_stage(correlation_id, stage, data):
    # structured logs are actually queryable
    logs.append({
        "correlation_id": correlation_id,
        "stage": stage,
        "data": data,
    })

def run_pipeline(query):
    # correlation IDs link logs across stages
    correlation_id = str(uuid.uuid4())[:8]

    safe_query = redact(query)
    log_stage(correlation_id, "query", {"text": safe_query})

    retrieved_ids = ["c1", "c3"]
    log_stage(correlation_id, "retrieval", {"chunk_ids": retrieved_ids})

    answer = "The Falcon plan costs twenty dollars per month."
    log_stage(correlation_id, "generation", {"answer": answer})

    return correlation_id, answer

correlation_id, answer = run_pipeline("What is my account number linked plan cost?")
print(f"Answer: {answer}")

print("\nLogs for this request:")
for entry in logs:
    if entry["correlation_id"] == correlation_id:
        print(f" {entry}")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows three separate log entries, one per pipeline stage, all sharing the same correlation ID and with the sensitive account number query redacted, exactly the structured, correlated, and safe logging.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Writing free-form text logs instead of structured fields that can actually be queried later.
Logging raw queries and answers that contain sensitive information with no redaction.
Letting log storage grow indefinitely with no retention or rotation policy.
Omitting a correlation ID, making it hard to link a request's log entries across pipeline stages.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Logging records what actually happened for each individual request, in structured detail.
Monitoring tracks aggregate trends; logging captures one specific request's full detail.
Structured log fields can be filtered and searched, unlike free-form text logs.
Query, retrieved chunk IDs, and generated answer each deserve their own logged field.
Detailed logs let a developer reconstruct exactly what happened on a specific failed request.
Sensitive information in queries and answers needs redaction or access control before logging.
Every request adds another log record, requiring its own retention and rotation policy.
A shared correlation ID ties log entries from several pipeline stages back to one request.
